prompt.context: The mayor of NYC was just elected based on her platform of creating a more environmentally sustainable city. During her campaign, she set a mandate to reduce the city's emissions by 80% by 2050. Critics are skeptical of these lofty goals. But the mayor is determined to make this her number one priority and has hired your firm to design the city's greenhouse gas reduction plan.
prompt.question: What factors would you consider when designing NYC's greenhouse gas reduction plan?

clarifying_info.q: Is there a specific budget for this plan?
clarifying_info.a: There is no specific budget, but the mayor doesn't want the plan to require an increase in taxes for her constituents.

clarifying_info.q: Does the plan cover the state of New York or just NYC?
clarifying_info.a: The plan is just focused on NYC, not the state of NY.

clarifying_info.q: Are there any constraints on the types of ideas to consider?
clarifying_info.a: The mayor is open to any and all ideas, so get creative.

clarifying_info.q: How does emissions trading / cap-and-trade work?
clarifying_info.a: It's a market-based approach to controlling pollution where a central authority allocates a limited number of permits that allow a discharge of a specific quantity of pollution. Polluters that want to emit beyond their allocated permits must buy permits from other polluters or pay a penalty.

clarifying_info.q: What is a LEED certified building?
clarifying_info.a: LEED (Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design) is the most widely used green building rating system in the world. LEED provides a framework for healthy, highly efficient, and cost-saving green buildings.

exhibits.title: NYC Greenhouse Gas Emissions
exhibits.shows: Three charts: (1) NYC GHG Emissions by Sector (breakdown of total emissions across sectors such as buildings and transportation), (2) NYC GHG Emissions from Large Buildings by End Use (breakdown of building emissions by use type, e.g. space heating, hot water, electricity), (3) Transportation Mode Shift for In-City Trips (trend showing how modes of transport are changing over time). Source: New York City Mayor's Office of Long-Term Planning and Sustainability.
exhibits.data: Sector breakdown highlights buildings (residential and commercial) as the dominant source of emissions; within buildings, space heating is the largest end-use category; transportation shows a trend toward more sustainable modes over time.

framework: 1. Design Plan — (a) GHG reduction initiatives: clean generation (renewables, carbon offsets, nuclear, clean fossil fuels) and reducing usage at the source (buildings, cars, industrial plants); (b) Cost considerations: government administrative costs, risk of driving businesses away, increase in cost of living

2. Implementation — (a) Who's involved: lobbyists, politicians, public; (b) Who's paying for additional costs: property managers, government subsidies, public; (c) How will it be enforced: tracking emissions, penalties
3. Benchmarking — (a) Programs implemented in other cities; (b) NYC's current GHG reduction progress; (c) Effectiveness of NYC's past initiatives

questions.prompt: Q2: The mayor heard that emissions trading (carbon cap-and-trade) is gaining popularity in Europe and select US cities. How would an emissions trading policy impact the city? Discuss pros and cons.
questions.guidance: Candidate should use a structured pros/cons approach. Pros: (1) Market-based flexibility for polluters to meet targets; (2) Ensures the city will meet targets; (3) Program can be self-funded through penalty fees; (4) Already tested in other markets and shown to be effective. Cons: (1) Logistically challenging to ensure compliance and enforcement; (2) Could involve politicking when allocating permits; (3) Could drive businesses out of the city by raising cost of doing business; (4) Could increase cost of living, disproportionately harming the poor.

questions.prompt: Q3: Based on Exhibit 1, where should the emissions trading program focus its efforts?
questions.guidance: Candidate should walk through the exhibit in a structured top-down manner. Average candidate: (1) Buildings are responsible for most emissions, primarily residential; (2) Space heating is the largest source of emissions for buildings; (3) Transportation has significant emissions but is becoming more sustainable and should not be the initial focus. Strong candidate adds: (1) It will likely be harder to reduce emissions from residential buildings because ownership is fragmented and there are a large number of them; (2) Buildings provide the largest opportunity but buildings alone may not be enough to achieve the 80% reduction target; (3) Targeting residential buildings could result in higher rent, disproportionately impacting the poor. No math is necessary.

questions.prompt: Q4: The mayor expects that NYC property owners will pass on additional costs to tenants. What factors would you consider when designing and implementing an emissions trading program?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm using a structured design vs. implementation split. Design considerations: (1) How to determine emission allotments; (2) How many phases to allow property owners enough time to make necessary upgrades; (3) Including additional flexibility for buildings with affordable housing units. Implementation considerations: (1) Community outreach to get buy-in from property owners; (2) Ensuring a robust platform to track emissions; (3) Creating an agency that enforces penalties.

questions.prompt: Q5 (optional): NYC has a long history of outside interests buying influence in City Hall. The client insists on a transparent process. How do we ensure the design phase is completely transparent to the public to avoid lobbying interests?
questions.guidance: Candidate should use a structured approach. Communication to Public: (1) Clear and timely press release schedule; (2) Weekly press conferences open to questions from reporters; (3) Town hall meetings. Process Control: (1) Restriction on any lobbying meetings; (2) Transparent and immediate release of any potential conflicts of interest; (3) Set guidelines for success online anchored to scientific data and guidance; (4) Remove politicians from the process.

questions.prompt: Q6 (optional): The client has decided to continue with cap-and-trade long-term but realizes it won't meet short-term emissions targets. The client is evaluating subsidies for builders of LEED certified buildings. What are the pros and cons of offering subsidies?
questions.guidance: Pros: (1) Will help get city to short-term emission targets; (2) Developers are already familiar with the LEED certification process; (3) Aligns incentives between city (reduce GHG) and property owners (save on energy bills); (4) Can benefit developers who can use LEED as a marketing tool. Cons: (1) Expensive for developers, who might look at other cities for projects; (2) Not the most effective way to reduce GHG — focuses on a single source and depends on LEED standards; (3) Doesn't address current buildings, so doesn't actually reduce existing GHG emissions; (4) Zoning and construction restrictions in NYC limit ability to implement quickly.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors would you consider when designing and implementing an emissions trading program for NYC, given that property owners will likely pass costs to tenants?

categories.name: Design Considerations
ideas: How to determine the emission allotments for each property
How many phases to allow property owners time to upgrade
Including additional flexibility provisions for buildings with affordable housing units

categories.name: Implementation Considerations
ideas: Community outreach to get buy-in from property owners
Building a robust platform to track emissions reporting
Creating an enforcement agency to impose and collect penalties

categories.name: Stakeholder & Transparency Considerations
ideas: Restricting lobbying meetings during the design phase
Immediate disclosure of any conflicts of interest
Removing politicians from the core design process
Town halls and press conferences for public communication

categories.name: Supplementary Policy (LEED subsidies)
ideas: Subsidies for new LEED-certified construction to hit short-term targets
Risk of deterring developers if subsidy is insufficient
Program does not address existing building stock

recommendation: Focus the emissions trading program primarily on residential and commercial buildings, with space heating as the priority end use, as this represents the largest share of NYC's GHG emissions
Pair the cap-and-trade program with short-term LEED construction subsidies to bridge the gap to near-term targets, while building out the tracking and enforcement infrastructure in phases
risks: Fragmented residential building ownership makes compliance monitoring difficult
Higher rents resulting from pass-through costs disproportionately harm low-income residents
Political interference in permit allocation could undermine program effectiveness
Businesses may relocate to avoid compliance costs
next_steps: Design phased permit allocation with affordable housing carve-outs
Establish an independent emissions tracking and enforcement agency
Launch community outreach and stakeholder engagement campaign
Benchmark against cap-and-trade programs in other cities (e.g., RGGI, EU ETS)
